summary: GMPLS lets each network element handle discovery, routing and signaling in a distributed way. Software-defined transport lets groups of elements be managed by centralized controllers. This informational document discusses how the two approaches can interwork.

eli5.summary: Some networks run by each device deciding for itself, and others by a central boss. This explains how both styles can work in one network.

questions: how do gmpls and centralized controllers cooperate
what are the benefits of hybrid control planes
how do controllers and gmpls elements exchange information
subtitle: How distributed and centralized network control systems work together in transport networks.

tldr.problem: Transport networks face challenges from multiple domains, vendors, and technologies. Network operators need both distributed local control (for responsiveness) and centralized management (for global optimization).
tldr.mechanism: GMPLS enables network elements to discover topology, compute paths, and signal connections locally and independently. Centralized controllers like ACTN orchestrate multiple domains while allowing GMPLS elements to handle their internal control.
tldr.outcome: By combining distributed GMPLS control with centralized SDN controller hierarchies, networks can achieve local resilience and fast reaction while maintaining global coordination and policy control.

today: RFC 9730 is an Informational RFC describing the interworking of GMPLS and centralized controller systems as of March 2025. It documents how both control approaches can coexist and coordinate in modern transport networks. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Two Control Planes in Transport Networks
sections.content:
Modern transport networks must manage multiple domains, hardware vendors, and technologies simultaneously. Two fundamentally different control approaches have emerged. GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) extends MPLS to support different switching types—time-division multiplex (TDM), wavelength (optical), and fiber switching—with each network element running a distributed control plane that discovers topology, computes paths, and establishes connections independently.

Meanwhile, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) introduces centralized controllers that collect network information and provision services from a central point. One example is ACTN (Abstraction and Control of Traffic-Engineered Networks), which defines a hierarchy of controllers at different levels: a Provisioning Network Controller (PNC) for a single domain, a Multi-Domain Service Coordinator (MDSC) managing multiple PNCs, and a Customer Network Controller (CNC) at the application level.

Rather than competing, these two approaches can complement each other. Centralized controllers can orchestrate multi-domain policies while allowing GMPLS-enabled domains to handle their own distributed signaling and recovery. This document describes how they can work together effectively.
sections.eli5: Some network elements are smart and can make local decisions quickly. Other controllers can see the whole network and plan for the future. Both work better when they cooperate rather than fight each other.

sections.title: GMPLS Control Plane Operations
sections.content:
The GMPLS control plane performs three key functions at each network element. Link discovery uses the Link Management Protocol (LMP) to verify connectivity and correlate link properties between neighboring nodes. Topology collection uses routing protocols like OSPF-TE (OSPF with traffic-engineering extensions) or IS-IS-TE to flood link-state advertisements throughout a domain, allowing each element to build a consistent view of network topology and resources.

Path computation and signaling allow network elements to calculate routes and establish Label Switched Paths (LSPs). A GMPLS element can compute paths locally based on its Traffic Engineering Database (TED) or request computation from a centralized Path Computation Element (PCE). RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering) then signals the path hop-by-hop, with each element allocating labels to establish the LSP.

GMPLS assumes each element has sufficient information to make good local decisions and can recover from failures through protection switching and restoration mechanisms defined in the control plane. This distributed approach provides fast failover but requires all elements to maintain consistent topology information.
sections.eli5: Each GMPLS device learns about its neighbors, builds a map of the network, plans a route, and sets up the connection by talking to the next hop. If something breaks, it quickly switches to a backup path.

sections.title: Centralized Controller Architecture
sections.content:
Centralized controllers like ACTN operate at a higher level of abstraction. A PNC collects topology and resource information from all network elements in a single domain. In GMPLS domains, the PNC passively listens to routing protocol messages (OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE) or actively retrieves topology using NETCONF and YANG modules. From non-GMPLS domains, the controller uses management protocols to discover topology.

The PNC abstraction capabilities let it present a simplified view of the domain to higher-level controllers. An MDSC coordinates multiple PNCs, receiving abstract topologies and determining multi-domain paths. The MDSC can compute end-to-end service routes using its global view, then decompose the service request into per-domain segments that the PNCs establish.

Controllers communicate with network elements and each other using multiple protocols: NETCONF/RESTCONF with YANG modules for configuration and topology retrieval, PCEP (PCE Communication Protocol) for path computation requests, and RSVP-TE for LSP setup in GMPLS domains. This hierarchical architecture enables scalability and supports different technologies and vendors within each domain.
sections.eli5: Controllers see the full network topology and can plan the best routes across many domains. Each controller talks to its domain's devices using standard messages, and higher controllers coordinate between domains.

sections.title: Interworking Mechanisms
sections.content:
GMPLS and centralized controllers use several approaches to interwork. For topology synchronization, a PNC managing a GMPLS domain listens to IGP routing protocol messages to learn topology in real time, or uses NETCONF to fetch topology from YANG modules. When topology changes occur, the GMPLS control plane disseminates updates to all elements, and the PNC reports the new state to the MDSC.

Path computation and service provisioning can happen at multiple levels. A centralized controller may compute the full end-to-end path across multiple domains and then request each domain's PNC to establish its segment. Alternatively, controllers can use PCEP to request path computation from PCEs, and the GMPLS elements themselves can compute paths using their local TEDs. For GMPLS domains, the PNC can trigger a source node to initiate an RSVP-TE session, allowing the distributed protocol to establish the path with local label allocation decisions.

Multi-domain service setup typically involves two methods: end-to-end RSVP-TE sessions (where border nodes exchange labels across domain boundaries) or LSP stitching (where each domain creates its own segment and the controller stitches them together with stitching labels). For non-GMPLS domains or where signaling doesn't traverse domains, controllers assign inter-domain labels and include them in setup messages.
sections.eli5: Controllers and GMPLS elements work together by sharing topology information and coordinating who computes which path. Controllers handle the big picture; GMPLS elements handle setting up the actual connections.

sections.title: Multi-Layer Networks and Recovery
sections.content:
In multi-layer transport networks (such as client-layer services running on server-layer optical infrastructure), GMPLS and centralized controllers coordinate across layers. An orchestrator at the multi-layer level coordinates a higher-layer controller and a lower-layer controller. When a higher-layer LSP requires resources, the orchestrator can pre-provision lower-layer Hierarchical LSPs (H-LSPs) that act as virtual links, or trigger their dynamic creation on demand.

Recovery in hybrid systems combines both approaches' strengths. For link protection (protecting individual hops), GMPLS mechanisms like Automatic Protection Switching operate at the data plane level. For path protection, the centralized controller can compute disjoint working and protecting paths using its global topology view. In single-domain GMPLS failures, distributed restoration mechanisms (pre-planned protection or Fast Reroute) provide quick recovery without waiting for controller intervention. For multi-domain failures, controllers can compute and establish replacement paths or orchestrate recovery across domains.

This hybrid approach offers speed (distributed mechanisms for local failures) with optimization (centralized planning for global resources). The interworking RFC outlines how each recovery mechanism—span protection, LSP protection, restoration, and rerouting—applies in different scenarios, from single-domain cases where GMPLS operates independently to multi-domain cases where controllers coordinate.
sections.eli5: When using layers of networks, controllers set up virtual links in the lower layer so the upper layer can use them. When something breaks, GMPLS elements can fix it fast locally, but controllers can plan better backup routes across the whole network.
